# Conclusion

Young people growing up in unequal societies receive a double message from schooling. They are told, insistently, that effort and talent are the legitimate basis of reward and that education is the route to a better life; they observe, just as insistently, that family resources and social connections shape who actually gets ahead [@resh_sense_2014; @traini_stratification_2022; @goudeau_hidden_2017a]. This article set out to understand how young people hold these two messages together — and what happens to that configuration as they accumulate experience of the educational system. Drawing on two-wave panel data (2023–2024) on Chilean students aged 11 to 16, and extending Castillo et al.'s [-@castillo_multidimensional_2023] multidimensional framework to a young population for the first time, we examined whether young people distinguish merit from privilege and descriptive judgments ("what is") from normative ones ("what should be"), whether these orientations are stable within individuals over time, and whether their meaning holds constant across school stages.

The answer to the first question is clear: young people do not hold a single pro- or anti-meritocratic attitude but four distinguishable orientations — perceived meritocracy, perceived privilege, meritocratic preferences, and privilege acceptance — and endorsement of merit coexists with recognition of structural advantage rather than displacing it. Most strikingly, perceived privilege is positively associated with stronger meritocratic preferences: recognizing unfair advantages intensifies, rather than extinguishes, the demand that rewards should follow merit, a normative-reactive pattern that unidimensional instruments would obscure [@castillo_multidimensional_2023; @wiesner_effort_2026; @mijs_visualizing_2026]. The developmental evidence is equally informative on both of its fronts. Within individuals, these orientations are measured equivalently over a one-year window, providing a reliable basis for interpreting over-time change as substantive rather than artifactual. Across school stages, however, equivalence breaks down precisely where theory would predict: the perception that "effort is rewarded" does not carry the same meaning for primary and secondary students, consistent with developmental accounts in which cumulative schooling experience progressively reshapes how young people interpret meritocratic signals [@allen_top_2016; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. In capturing these distinctions among young people themselves, the approach moves beyond the most recent dedicated alternative, the teacher-focused, perception-only scale of @chauvin_school_2026, toward a measure of how youth distinguish merit from privilege and description from preference.

These findings sharpen how meritocracy effects in educational contexts should be interpreted. By distinguishing dimensions that unidimensional measures collapse, the four-factor model shows that part of what is often read as young people's declining belief in meritocracy may instead reflect growing recognition of structural constraints alongside stable — even strengthening — merit endorsement [@reynolds_perceptions_2014a; @zhu_meritocratic_2025; @liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025]. It also offers a distinct route to the coexistence of contrasting beliefs: where typological approaches document that coexistence by sorting individuals into attitudinal clusters [@kwon_multidimensionality_2024; @zhu_meritocratic_2025], the present study represents it within a single measurement model that supports longitudinal inference, rather than requiring person-centered classification. The combination of strict longitudinal invariance and cross-level non-invariance establishes a key boundary condition: within-person comparisons over time are warranted, whereas comparisons across school stages must account for the shifting meaning of perceived meritocracy.

Although this study draws on a single country, its contributions carry implications beyond the Chilean case. Three findings are likely to travel across educational systems. First, the conceptual distinction between perceived and preferred meritocracy, and between meritocratic and privilege-based principles, reflects general cognitive and normative capacities that develop during adolescence regardless of national context; the four-factor structure should therefore replicate in other highly stratified systems. Second, the coexistence of merit endorsement and recognition of privilege, the core pattern underlying dual consciousness, has been documented in China [@liu_does_2025; @tang_meritocratic_2025], the United States and Finland [@zhu_meritocratic_2025], and Europe [@kwon_multidimensionality_2024], suggesting it is not a Chilean peculiarity. Third, the logic of longitudinal invariance testing as a prerequisite for developmental inference is methodologically general and applies to any panel study of young people's beliefs. By contrast, the specific pattern of cross-cohort non-invariance, concentrated in perceived effort, may be more system-dependent: it likely reflects the particular intensity and timing of school-based sorting in Chile's tracked and marketized system. Future research in countries with different tracking regimes and stratification profiles will help clarify which aspects of measurement equivalence are universal and which are conditioned by institutional features.

Beyond measurement, the findings speak to how young people's relationship to meritocracy — and to the institutions that promote it — should be understood. Young people emerge from this study not as passive recipients of meritocratic ideology but as active interpreters of institutional narratives about fairness, who navigate the tension between what schools tell them and what they observe, and whose interpretive frames grow more critical as schooling advances. This reframing matters for how their beliefs are read in education and citizenship debates alike. The young person who recognizes privilege while demanding merit-based rewards is not cynical or disengaged; they are articulating an incipient civic claim about justice, one that schools and civic education can engage as a resource rather than treat as a deficit to correct. And the finding that perceived privilege intensifies meritocratic preferences carries a pointed implication for educational systems themselves: young people who see that rewards do not follow merit do not abandon the ideal of fairness — they demand it more strongly. Systems that sustain a strong meritocratic discourse while visibly reproducing inequality thus risk widening the gap between what they promise and what young people experience, with consequences that extend beyond school walls to institutional trust, sense of justice, and civic engagement — the terrain on which the legitimacy of educational institutions is contested by youth themselves.

This study has limitations that point to clear directions for future research. The scale is deliberately minimalist, with two items per factor, which constrains content coverage and reliability and means that claims about subtle within-dimension differences should be treated with caution. Future work should expand and refine the item pool, adding at least one additional indicator per factor and testing whether richer item sets alter the invariance conclusions reported here. With only two waves and two school levels, additional waves and broader age coverage are needed to better trace developmental trajectories and identify when shifts in the meaning of perceived meritocracy occur. Cross-level non-invariance calls for differential item functioning analyses and stage-sensitive item formulations to support comparability across educational stages. Most importantly, future research should examine how these orientations relate to the outcomes for which they are most likely to matter in young people's lives: their sense of justice and fairness, civic attitudes and engagement, trust in institutions, and wellbeing, alongside academic motivation. By establishing that young people's beliefs about merit and privilege can be measured reliably, multidimensionally, and equivalently over time, this study offers a firmer foundation for understanding how the meritocratic promise is received, questioned, and reinterpreted across youth — and for taking seriously what young people's evolving sense of fairness reveals about the institutions that shape their lives.
